reason: The majority expressly held and applied the Section 129 requirement of knowing dealing in dutiable goods with intent to defraud revenue.
The statement is an overbroad formulation drawn from a quoted earlier case rather than this court's own precise Land Acquisition Ordinance holding.
The court did hold that vesting under the Land Acquisition Ordinance creates a new Crown title, but the statement drops the material Section 12(1) vesting condition.
The majority held that the note was payable at a determinable future time and required the higher promissory-note stamp.
The majority held that the insufficiently stamped promissory note was inadmissible under section 41 and could not found the action.
The headnote itself marks the title-proof proposition as obiter and the quote relies on an earlier case rather than the majority holding.
The holding was confined to treating an executor de son tort as a legal representative for section 341 execution, not as a general legal representative for all purposes.
The court decided the quantum point on the basis that alimony pendente lite ended on the husband's death.
The judgment directly addressed the consequence of default under section 63(3), so the statement saying it was not addressed is wrong.
The actual holding was narrowly about striking off a claim for default in prepayment of costs, while the statement says only vague unspecified orders.
The court expressly held that the State may take advantage of the Prescription Ordinance.
The court held that P19 was not an acknowledgment of the plaintiff's claim and therefore did not defeat prescription.
The court held that uncertainty of title to the trust property was the condition permitting a section 112(1) vesting order.
The quote concerns uncertainty of title and a vesting order, not any rule that a trust can be created under the Trusts Ordinance.
The court decided the custom for this particular Badrakali Kovil and preserved other male descendants' poosari rights, which the statement omits.
The judgment held the opposite: the lapse principle had no application on the facts because the property was given on trust.
The court held that an ex facie duly executed Indian power of attorney attracted the section 85 presumption.
The court applied the rule that cancellation of a lease requires grave misuse and found the proved damage insufficient.
The cross-appeal was allowed because the parties' rights had to be determined as at the date the action was instituted.
The statement confuses the Buddhist Temporalities Ordinance with the prescription issue and does not state the court's actual holding.
The court applied Evidence Ordinance section 95, but only because the assessment numbers and evidence gave a definite description of the land intended to pass.
The deed failed because the maker had never acted as Viharadhipathi and acted during the true Viharadhipathi's lifetime, not because every Viharadhipathi lacks appointment power.
The court held that D2 by itself did not prove surrender or abandonment and could operate only as an appointment of a successor.
The court held that the combined section 247 and Paulian action could not be instituted without the required Conciliation Board certificate.
The court's inherent-power holding was limited to correcting its own procedural notice mistake by pronouncing the same judgment afresh.
